relationship: lament over apparent divine delay amid oppression
rationale: Habakkuk asks how long he must cry while wronged without being heard or saved. The psalm likewise repeatedly asks how long the Lord will turn away, then asks Him to hear lest the enemy prevail. Both voice distressed waiting for divine help.

relationship: wrongdoing encountered in the place of judgment
rationale: Habakkuk complains of misery and impiety, with judgment against him and a judge who takes. Ecclesiastes likewise observes an ungodly person in the place of judgment and righteousness. Both locate wrongdoing where justice should be administered.

relationship: judgment distorted or driven back
rationale: Habakkuk describes scattered law and distorted judgment while the impious oppresses the righteous. Isaiah likewise says judgment was driven backward, righteousness withdrew and the Lord was displeased at the absence of judgment. Both connect public injustice with the failure of judgment.

relationship: explicit later quotation of an unbelievable divine work
rationale: Habakkuk addresses despisers and announces a work they will not believe even when recounted. Acts explicitly warns about what the prophets spoke and repeats the address, wonder and vanishing, and the work that will not be believed. The wording directly connects the warning.

relationship: the Lord brings an invading nation
rationale: Habakkuk announces the Lord raising Chaldean warriors who seize dwellings not their own. Jeremiah likewise announces a distant nation brought against Israel to consume its produce and attack fortified cities. Both present the invading force within a divine announcement, without assigning Jeremiah Habakkuk's national label.

relationship: an imperial force claims authority for itself
rationale: Habakkuk describes the invaders' judgment and claim proceeding from themselves. Isaiah quotes the Assyrian ruler crediting his own strength and wisdom for seizing nations without resistance. Both expose the conqueror's self-assertion, in distinct descriptions of imperial power.

relationship: a distant invading nation compared to an eagle
rationale: Habakkuk describes horsemen rushing from afar and flying like an eagle eager to eat. Deuteronomy likewise announces a nation from afar coming like an eagle's swoop. The distance and predatory flight imagery connect the threats.

relationship: the gathering of large numbers of captives
rationale: Habakkuk pictures the invading force gathering captives like sand. Kings recounts Babylon's king deporting rulers, warriors and craftsmen in large stated numbers. The historical account illustrates mass deportation without equating its numerical totals with the sand comparison.

relationship: siege works used against fortified cities
rationale: Habakkuk says the invaders mock fortresses, throw up a mound and seize them. Ezekiel's oracle names Babylon's king and describes building around Tyre, enclosing it with a palisade and weapons, and throwing down its walls. Both portray siege construction overcoming defenses.

relationship: same-book recognition of strength as God's
rationale: Habakkuk 1:11 concludes that this strength belongs to the speaker's God. The final verse likewise calls the Lord God the speaker's strength. This explicit shared attribution is retained without changing 1:11's preceding spirit and propitiation wording.

relationship: a hostile power appointed within divine judgment
rationale: Habakkuk addresses the Lord as having appointed the threatening figure for judgment. Isaiah likewise calls Assyria a rod of divine anger, while distinguishing the ruler's destructive intention. The connection concerns the power's assigned role, not agreement with every purpose of the invader.

relationship: the difficulty of wicked prosperity beside righteous suffering
rationale: Habakkuk questions God's silence when the impious swallows the righteous. The psalm likewise places prosperous sinners beside the speaker's apparently vain righteousness and daily scourging. Both articulate the distress caused by the apparent advantage of the wicked.

relationship: people pictured as vulnerable fish
rationale: Habakkuk likens people to fish without a leader, before describing their capture. Ecclesiastes likewise compares people caught by an evil time to fish in an evil net. Both use the vulnerability of fish to describe human exposure to harm.

relationship: the catching of people represented as fishing
rationale: Habakkuk depicts a whole catch hauled by hook, casting net and seines, continuing the comparison of people with fish. Jeremiah likewise describes fishermen sent to fish for the people, followed by hunters and repayment for wrongdoing. Both apply fishing to the taking of people, with distinct agents and instruments.

relationship: worship directed to material things associated with food and benefit
rationale: Habakkuk says the captors sacrifice to nets because these provide their rich food. Isaiah describes wood used for warmth and cooking, with the rest fashioned into a god and worshiped. Both expose worship directed toward material means of benefit, while the actions upon the material differ.

relationship: same-book accusation of destructive action against nations and its consequence
rationale: Habakkuk 1:17 describes continuing to cast the net and kill nations without sparing them. The later woe charges the despoiling of many nations and bloodshed, then promises the remaining peoples will despoil the aggressor. The later accusation and reversal answer the earlier portrayal of unchecked harm.

relationship: prophetic waiting represented by a watcher's station
rationale: Habakkuk stands at his watch to look for what God will speak. Isaiah likewise receives an instruction to station a watcher, who stands day and night and reports what is seen and heard from the Lord. Both use the watcher's position for attentive reception of a message.

relationship: a prophetic message committed to a tablet
rationale: Habakkuk is commanded to write the vision clearly on a boxwood tablet for its readers. Isaiah likewise is commanded to write on a tablet and in a book so that the words endure. Both explicitly require a written record, with different stated purposes and materials.

relationship: later use of the coming-one promise to encourage endurance
rationale: Habakkuk commands waiting if he delays because the coming one will come and not linger. Hebrews likewise urges endurance before repeating that the coming One will come and not delay. Both place the promise within an exhortation to patient expectation.

relationship: later quotation joining righteous life and the danger of drawing back
rationale: Habakkuk says God's soul takes no pleasure in one drawing back and that the righteous one lives by My faithfulness. Hebrews repeats both clauses in reversed order, saying My righteous one lives by faith. The connection preserves the distinct placement of My and the native faithfulness wording.

relationship: explicit later use of the righteous-one life statement
rationale: Habakkuk declares that the righteous one lives by My faithfulness. Romans introduces Scripture saying the righteous one lives by faith within its account of the gospel and God's righteousness. The shared statement is direct, while Habakkuk's possessive and faithfulness wording remain distinct.

relationship: later use of the righteous-one statement in discussion of law and faith
rationale: Habakkuk says the righteous one lives by My faithfulness. Galatians quotes the righteous one living by faith while arguing about justification before God and law. The later argumentative use is recorded without silently replacing the source's My faithfulness wording.

relationship: insatiable human appetite compared to Hades
rationale: Habakkuk portrays the boastful conqueror's appetite as Hades and death, never filled despite gathered peoples. Proverbs likewise says Hades and destruction are not filled and compares them with insatiable human eyes. Both expressly link human insatiability with Hades.

relationship: a saying taken up against an oppressive ruler
rationale: Habakkuk announces a parable and riddle taken up against one accumulating what is not his. Isaiah likewise introduces a lament against Babylon's king after release from harsh slavery and describes the taskmaster's end. Both turn the oppressor into the subject of a public saying after exploitation.

relationship: same-chapter plunder threatened and explained as reversal
rationale: Habakkuk 2:7 tells the addressed oppressor that he will become plunder when adversaries rise. The following verse explains that remaining peoples will despoil him because he despoiled many nations. The next unit gives the explicit reciprocal reason for the threatened loss.

relationship: recompense corresponding to harm done to others
rationale: Habakkuk says the despoiler of many nations will himself be despoiled by remaining peoples. Obadiah likewise announces that what was done will return upon the doer's own head. Both explicitly state reciprocal judgment, with Habakkuk specifying plunder and bloodshed.

relationship: a high nest imagined as security from danger
rationale: Habakkuk condemns setting a nest high to escape evils while acquiring evil gain. Obadiah likewise describes a high dwelling, imagined security from being brought down and a nest among stars from which God will bring its occupant down. Both challenge safety sought through elevated habitation.

relationship: a house established through wrongdoing becomes an accusation
rationale: Habakkuk says the plot brought shame upon the house and involved the end of many peoples. Jeremiah likewise condemns a house built without righteousness, unpaid labor, greed and innocent blood. Both connect the household's apparent advancement with culpable harm.

relationship: stones given the role of crying out
rationale: Habakkuk depicts a stone crying from a wall and a beetle from wood uttering words. Jesus likewise says that stones will cry out if the disciples fall silent. The personified stone's speech is shared; the settings differ, and no beam is substituted for Habakkuk's beetle.

relationship: building a city with bloodshed and injustice
rationale: Habakkuk condemns building a city with bloodshed and preparing it with injustices. Micah likewise addresses leaders who build Zion with bloodshed and Jerusalem with injustices. The distinctive paired accusation directly connects the passages.

relationship: earth filled with knowledge of the Lord compared to covering waters
rationale: Habakkuk announces the earth filled with knowing the Lord's glory as water covers. Isaiah likewise declares the whole earth filled with knowledge of the Lord as abundant water covers the seas. Both combine universal knowledge of God with the covering-water comparison.

relationship: the cup of divine judgment passes to those who harmed others
rationale: Habakkuk commands the aggressor to drink dishonor because the cup from the Lord's right hand has reached him. Isaiah describes the Lord's cup of anger taken from Jerusalem and thrown into its oppressors' hands. Both portray judgment through a cup reaching wrongdoers.

relationship: same-chapter repeated indictment for bloodshed and impiety
rationale: Both units expressly accuse the addressed power of human bloodshed and impiety against land, city and all inhabitants. The repeated charge connects the woes while 2:17 also names Lebanon and wild animals, details absent from 2:8.

relationship: the futility of worshiping objects made by their worshipers
rationale: Habakkuk questions the use of carved and cast objects and the maker's trust in mute idols. Isaiah likewise calls fashioned gods useless and narrates a craftsman making an image from wood and worshiping it. Both expose reliance on human fabrication.

relationship: wood adorned with precious metal cannot act as a living being
rationale: Habakkuk mocks calling wood to wake and stone to rise, describing a gold-and-silver plate with no breath. Jeremiah likewise describes worked wood adorned with gold and silver, unable to move or take a step. Both oppose the decorated object to the powers expected of life.

relationship: cast images have no living spirit
rationale: Habakkuk explicitly says the decorated image has no breath at all. Jeremiah likewise says cast objects are false and have no spirit in them, then calls them futile works that perish. Both deny life to the fabricated object.

relationship: the Lord located in His holy sanctuary
rationale: Habakkuk contrasts mute idols with the Lord in His holy sanctuary. The psalm likewise places the Lord in His holy temple, with His throne in heaven and eyes examining people. Both explicitly identify His holy dwelling, while Habakkuk calls the earth to reverence.

relationship: mercy remembered in the face of divine wrath
rationale: Habakkuk declares that God will remember mercy in wrath when his soul is troubled. The psalm likewise asks whether God will forget pity or shut His compassions in wrath, then recalls the Lord's works. This connection concerns mercy and wrath, without interpreting the two living creatures.

relationship: divine appearance described as coming from a mountain region
rationale: Habakkuk depicts God coming from Teman and the Holy One from a shaded mountain, with excellence covering heaven. Deuteronomy likewise describes the Lord coming from Sinai, appearing from Seir and hastening from Mount Paran. The mountain-coming pattern is shared without equating the named locations.

relationship: brightness in the description of divine glory
rationale: Habakkuk describes divine brightness like light, followed by horns in His hands and mighty love. Ezekiel likewise depicts brightness around the visible likeness of the Lord's glory, comparing it to a bow in cloud. The link concerns radiance, without treating the other visionary details as identical.

relationship: earth and mountains shaken and peoples melted before God
rationale: Habakkuk describes the earth shaking, nations melting and mountains crushed. Nahum likewise depicts mountains and earth shaken, rulers melted by fury and rocks crushed. Both present divine presence through these combined images of shaking, melting and crushing.

relationship: terror and flight in Midian's camp
rationale: Habakkuk says the tents of Midian will be terrified. Judges narrates panic and flight in the camp identified earlier as Midian's, with the Lord setting swords against neighbors. The narrative supplies a particular example of Midianite camp terror, without asserting that Habakkuk identifies this event exclusively.

relationship: salvation associated with God's passage through waters
rationale: Habakkuk questions fury against rivers and sea and calls God's riding salvation. The psalm recalls the redemption of His people, fearful waters and depths, and His way in the sea. Both combine divine passage through waters with the people's deliverance.

relationship: God depicted bending a bow for judgment
rationale: Habakkuk pictures God bending His bow against scepters. The psalm likewise presents God as righteous judge and describes Him bending a bow and preparing deadly arrows. The martial image portrays divine judgment, with different objects specified.

relationship: waters and depths described with sound during divine appearance
rationale: Habakkuk combines peoples' travail, scattered waters and the abyss giving voice in God's passage. The psalm likewise portrays waters seeing God in fear, troubled depths, sounding waters and clouds giving voice. Both animate the waters in the depiction of divine appearance.

relationship: sun and moon within an account of divine battle
rationale: Habakkuk describes the sun raised, the moon standing in its appointed place and bright weapons. Joshua's battle account likewise names the sun standing and the moon remaining still while the Lord fights for Israel. The common celestial and battle setting is retained, while Habakkuk's sun-raised wording is not changed.

relationship: divine fury directed against nations
rationale: Habakkuk describes nations brought down in divine fury and earth diminished by threat. Isaiah likewise summons nations and earth to hear because the Lord's wrath and anger are against nations to hand them to slaughter. Both explicitly connect judgment upon nations with divine fury.

relationship: salvation and mercy for God's anointed
rationale: Habakkuk describes God going out to save His people and His anointed ones. The psalm likewise magnifies His king's salvations and mercy to His anointed, David and his seed. The connection preserves the source's plural anointed ones and the psalm's specifically named royal recipient.

relationship: God's way through the sea's waters
rationale: Habakkuk pictures God's horses driven into the sea and troubling much water. The psalm likewise describes God's way in the sea and paths in many waters. Both portray divine movement through water, without assigning horses to the psalm.

relationship: bodily distress in response to a prophetic encounter
rationale: Habakkuk describes terror in his belly, trembling in his bones and a troubled bodily condition. Daniel likewise describes strong fear surrounding the vision and his own loss of strength and fall to the ground. Both describe the bodily effect of the encounter, with distinct sensations and accounts of sound.

relationship: failure of fields, vines and fig trees
rationale: Habakkuk lists failed figs, vines, olives and fields producing no food. Joel likewise describes failed grain, diminished oil and dried or diminished vines, figs and field trees. Both enumerate agricultural loss across several crops.

relationship: cattle and sheep without food
rationale: Habakkuk describes sheep failing for lack of food and no cattle at feeding troughs. Joel likewise says cattle have no pasture and sheep disappeared. The animals' food failure is a distinct shared element of the agricultural calamity.

relationship: rejoicing in God as Savior
rationale: Habakkuk declares that he will exult in the Lord and rejoice in God his Savior. Mary's song likewise magnifies the Lord and says her spirit rejoiced in God her Savior. The closely corresponding declaration links the two songs.

relationship: God's strength places the speaker's feet upon heights
rationale: Habakkuk names God as his strength, setting his feet toward completion and leading him onto heights. The psalm likewise describes divine power, a blameless way, firmly set feet and standing on heights. The shared cluster is retained without importing the psalm's deer comparison into Habakkuk.
